articles.title: Wipro Built a Whole Center to Run Claude. The Company That Sold Cheap Code Is Now Selling AI to Replace It.
articles.excerpt: The Bengaluru IT giant will certify 10,000 staff on Anthropic's models in 18 months — a defensive pivot that quietly redraws the career math for every Indian engineer who came up through the services pipeline.
articles.image_caption: Software engineers collaborating at a technology workspace, the kind of delivery floor Wipro is retraining around Anthropic's Claude models.
articles.nri_angle: For the hundreds of thousands of Indian engineers — and their relatives in the US and UK — who climbed out of the IT services pipeline that Wipro built, the company's bet on Claude is a signal that the old ladder of 'learn to code, get placed, get an H-1B' is being rebuilt around AI fluency rather than headcount.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's First Real Chip Fab Just Signed the Hardest Vendor in Tech. Now the Hard Part Begins.
articles.excerpt: Tata Electronics has locked in ASML lithography for its $11 billion Dholera fab, with first chips due by December — a milestone that turns India's semiconductor talk into a delivery deadline.
articles.image_caption: A close-up of a semiconductor processor die, the class of analog and logic chips Tata's Dholera fab aims to produce.
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin semiconductor engineers staff the design and process teams at Micron, Intel, AMD, Applied Materials and ASML's own customers — and a working fab in Gujarat is the first credible reason in a generation for some of them to consider building chips at home instead of abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Biggest Exchange Finally Filed to Go Public. At $57 Billion, NRIs Are About to Get a Piece of the Casino's House.
articles.excerpt: After years of regulatory delay, the National Stock Exchange filed IPO papers this week — a once-blocked listing that hands a $2.6 billion windfall to early backers and a rare shot at owning the rails of India's markets.
articles.image_caption: A stock market display board showing live price data, the kind of trading the NSE's platform processes as the world's most active derivatives exchange.
articles.nri_angle: NRIs have spent years pouring money into Indian stocks through the NSE's platform; its long-delayed IPO is the first realistic chance for diaspora investors — increasingly able to buy in via GIFT City and global brokerages — to own the exchange itself rather than just trade on it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Qualcomm Is Betting $10 Billion That the Phone Era Is Over. The Data Center Is the New Battleground.
articles.excerpt: The chipmaker is in talks to buy Tenstorrent and its star engineer Jim Keller, days before an investor day meant to convince Wall Street it can challenge Nvidia. For the Indian engineers who staff its chip-design ranks, it's a whole new product line.
articles.image_caption: Qualcomm President and CEO Cristiano Amon, who is steering the company toward data-center and edge-AI silicon
articles.nri_angle: Qualcomm employs thousands of Indian-origin chip engineers in the US and runs huge design centers in Bengaluru and Hyderabad; a pivot into data-center AI silicon reshapes the careers and job map for that workforce.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Sriram Krishnan Is Leaving the White House AI Job. The Diaspora Got a Seat at the Table — and a Lesson in Its Limits.
articles.excerpt: The most senior Indian-American voice on AI policy exits at the end of June, just as Washington restricts foreign access to frontier models and revives a $100,000 H-1B fee. Representation, it turns out, isn't the same as protection.
articles.image_caption: Sriram Krishnan, the outgoing Senior White House Policy Advisor on Artificial Intelligence
articles.nri_angle: An Indian-American held the top AI policy seat in the White House, but the administration's H-1B fee and foreign-national model restrictions hit Indian tech workers hardest — a pointed lesson on the gap between having representation and having protection.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: You Can Now Pay With UPI at a Department Store in Nice. India's Payment Rail Is Quietly Going Global.
articles.excerpt: Within weeks, UPI has gone live in France and Cambodia, pushing past eight countries for merchant payments. For the diaspora, the real prize isn't tourist convenience — it's faster, cheaper remittances.
articles.image_caption: India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI), the real-time payment rail now expanding to overseas merchants
articles.nri_angle: UPI's overseas rollout means NRIs get a familiar payment app abroad and, more importantly, cheaper instant cross-border remittances that threaten the fees of legacy money-transfer operators.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Tim Cook Says Your Next iPhone Costs More. Blame the AI Memory Crunch — and Thank an Indian CEO for It.
articles.excerpt: The same shortage driving Apple's price hikes is minting profits for Micron's Sanjay Mehrotra. The diaspora sits on both sides of the trade.
articles.image_caption: Micron Technology chairman, president and CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, the Indian-origin chip executive whose memory business is benefiting from the AI-driven shortage
articles.nri_angle: Indian American households buy a lot of Apple gear and will feel the price hikes, while the global memory crunch driving them is enriching Micron's Indian-origin CEO Sanjay Mehrotra and pulling India deeper into the chip supply chain.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Funded an AI That Watches the Country From Orbit. For the Diaspora, It's a New Kind of Homecoming.
articles.excerpt: A $2.6 million grant to Bengaluru's SatSure signals India's push for sovereign Earth-observation AI — and a first real career pitch to diaspora space scientists.
articles.image_caption: An earth-observation satellite; India is funding AI to monitor the country from orbit
articles.nri_angle: A large share of the global space and geospatial workforce is Indian; India's private space push and its bet on sovereign Earth-observation AI is the first credible come-home-or-invest pitch in their own field.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: SolarSquare Raised $53 Million to Put Power Plants on India's Rooftops. NRIs Already Own a Lot of Those Roofs.
articles.excerpt: The Mumbai startup's Series C is a bet that India's homeowners are done with load-shedding — and a quiet opportunity for the diaspora that owns property back home.
articles.image_caption: Rooftop solar panels on a home, the market SolarSquare is racing to capture across Indian cities
articles.nri_angle: Many NRIs own property in India — the family home or an investment flat — making them direct candidates for rooftop solar, while the sector is becoming a climate-infrastructure investment play backed by funds the diaspora already knows.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Google Paid $2.7 Billion to Bring Noam Shazeer Home. He Just Left for OpenAI.
articles.excerpt: The man who co-invented the transformer is changing sides again — and the AI talent war he embodies is quietly reshaping careers for thousands of Indian researchers on visas.
articles.image_caption: The Google sign at the Googleplex headquarters in Mountain View, California
articles.nri_angle: The AI talent war minting nine-figure offers runs on Indian-origin researchers, but for those on H-1B and O-1 visas, switching labs is a legal and financial gamble that the headline numbers hide.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Tech Hiring Just Hit a 28-Month Low. The Conveyor Belt That Built the Diaspora Is Jamming.
articles.excerpt: Active openings have fallen to 93,000 even as 56,000 professionals hunt for jobs — and the entry-level door, the one that fed a generation of H-1B careers, is closing fastest.
articles.image_caption: Aerial view of the glass pyramid at the Infosys campus in Bengaluru, India
articles.nri_angle: The campus-to-IT-major-to-US-onsite path that brought a generation of Indian Americans here is narrowing, reshaping the future H-1B pipeline and the family-reunification math behind it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Intel Is Shedding 25,000 Chip Engineers. For the Indian Diaspora, the Question Is Whether They Go Home.
articles.excerpt: The deep silicon talent America is laying off is exactly what Gujarat's new fabs need — and a 60-day visa clock is making the return-to-India math look rational.
articles.image_caption: A semiconductor wafer patterned with integrated circuit dies before packaging
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin engineers are over-represented in US chip design, so Intel's mass layoffs collide directly with India's semiconductor build-out — turning a 60-day H-1B grace period into a return-to-India decision.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: eBay Is Cutting 639 American Jobs While Filing for 429 H-1B Workers. Indians Will Wear the Backlash.
articles.excerpt: The e-commerce firm's own filings put layoffs and visa applications side by side — handing Washington exactly the ammunition it has been hunting for.
articles.image_caption: eBay's Silicon Valley headquarters in San Jose, California
articles.nri_angle: Indians get ~70% of H-1B visas, so when a company lays off Americans while filing for foreign workers, Indian professionals become the lightning rod in a political fight over corporate cost-cutting and AI automation.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Microsoft Just Shipped an AI That Finishes Your Work, Not Drafts It. Satya Nadella Warns It Could Hollow Out Industries.
articles.excerpt: Copilot Cowork goes global the same week its own CEO cautions that a few AI models could 'eat everything they see' — and Indian tech workers sit on both sides of that bet.
articles.image_caption: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella
articles.nri_angle: Cowork automates the multi-step office workflows that employ hundreds of thousands of Indians at firms like TCS and Cognizant, making Nadella's 'move up the stack' warning a direct career instruction for the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Accenture Reports Earnings Under an AI Cloud. The Company That Employs the Most Indians Is a Referendum on the Whole Sector.
articles.excerpt: Wall Street wants to know whether a business built on selling human hours can survive when the hours go machine-supplied — and lakhs of Indian careers ride on the answer.
articles.image_caption: Accenture's office building in Gachibowli, Hyderabad
articles.nri_angle: Accenture's largest employee base is in India and its US ops run heavily on Indian H-1B/L-1 talent, so its earnings double as a verdict on whether AI is hollowing out the mid-career IT jobs the diaspora climbed toward.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Satya Nadella Has a New Word for the AI Age: 'Token Capital.' It's a Warning Dressed as a Buzzword.
articles.excerpt: Microsoft's CEO says the winners won't own the smartest model — they'll own the learning loop. For India's engineers and IT giants, that reframes the whole AI threat.
articles.image_caption: Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella, who introduced the 'token capital' framework at Build 2026
articles.nri_angle: Nadella's 'token capital' framing recasts AI as a chance for India's IT majors and the diaspora's engineers to own institutional knowledge rather than be commoditised by it — a counter-narrative to the AI-layoff panic.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Adobe Beat Earnings and Hit a 7-Year Low. The CFO Left for a Chip Company. That Tells You Everything.
articles.excerpt: Shantanu Narayen's Adobe tripled its AI revenue and raised guidance — then watched its stock crater on a double leadership vacuum and a deeper fear about software's future.
articles.image_caption: Shantanu Narayen, Adobe's chief executive of 18 years, who has announced he will step down once a successor is named
articles.nri_angle: Adobe's stumble matters to the diaspora: Narayen is among the longest-serving Indian-origin Silicon Valley CEOs, and the firm's large India engineering base and H-1B staff are exposed to the strategic uncertainty now hanging over the company.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Biggest Brokerages Just Got Cleared to Sell You Apple and Nvidia. The Gateway Is a City in Gujarat.
articles.excerpt: Zerodha, Groww, Angel One and Upstox have IFSCA approval to offer direct US-stock access through GIFT City — collapsing the wall between Indian retail savers and Wall Street.
articles.image_caption: The GIFT One tower in Gujarat's GIFT City, the finance hub serving as the gateway for Indians to buy U.S. stocks (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: A cheaper, regulated channel for Indians to buy US stocks deepens the financial bridge NRIs straddle daily — and ties the Indian middle class directly to the Silicon Valley fortunes the diaspora helps build.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Zepto Wants to Be India's First Pure Quick-Commerce IPO. The Valuation Tells the Real Story.
articles.excerpt: The ten-minute delivery giant filed to raise ₹8,010 crore at a reported $7 billion — below rival Swiggy. For NRI investors, July's listing is a referendum on the cash-burn era.
articles.image_caption: Zepto, the quick-commerce startup pursuing India's first pure 10-minute-delivery IPO (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Zepto is the cleanest available bet on a uniquely Indian behaviour NRIs watch family members do daily, and its listing will tell diaspora angel investors whether growth-at-any-cost is finally over.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Is Done Pretending It Will Ban Crypto. It Has a Bigger Plan: Owning the Money Itself.
articles.excerpt: Coinbase just switched on rupee trading while the RBI repositions the digital rupee as strategic infrastructure. For the diaspora, the real story is cheaper remittances — and far tighter surveillance.
articles.image_caption: The Reserve Bank of India in Mumbai, which is building out the digital rupee as India pivots from banning crypto to issuing its own (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: A cross-border digital-rupee corridor could cut the cost of the $100B+ NRIs remit home each year, even as tighter KYC and geo-tagging make diaspora crypto moves fully visible and taxable.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Space Programme Is No Longer Just ISRO. For the Diaspora, That Changes the Bet.
articles.excerpt: A wave of state grants and $100 million in deep-tech deals signed in France point to a privatised space sector — and a new reason for NRI capital and engineers to look home.
articles.image_caption: Wikimedia Commons (CC)
articles.nri_angle: India's space story is shifting from a source of NRI pride to a source of NRI opportunity, with diaspora capital and returning engineers poised to fund the next generation of launch and Earth-observation startups.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The World's Cybersecurity Firms Are Quietly Moving to Bengaluru. India's Tech Job Map Is Being Redrawn.
articles.excerpt: As US visa fights make importing Indian engineers expensive, multinationals are building the jobs in India instead — and India's captive-center workforce is on track to hit 2.36 million this year.
articles.image_caption: Bengaluru, the city absorbing the bulk of India's new cybersecurity capability centers (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: For Indian engineers weighing whether the H-1B ladder is still worth climbing, the GCC boom signals that the best jobs at American firms may increasingly be in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, not Silicon Valley.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Startup Money Is Flowing Again — and This Week the Smart Capital Bet on Boring
articles.excerpt: A $30 million round for a consumer-AI startup backed by Airtel and PhonePe's CEO headlines a fourth straight week of funding gains, as investors pivot from hype to companies that actually make money.
articles.image_caption: Mumbai's financial skyline; Indian startup funding rebounded this week on bets in less flashy sectors (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: For NRI angel investors and the growing crowd putting diaspora money into Indian startups, the shift toward profitable, distribution-backed companies signals where the next decade of cross-border bets is heading.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Razorpay Files Quietly for a $600 Million IPO. The Valuation Cut Tells the Real Story.
articles.excerpt: Bengaluru's biggest payments gateway is targeting a year-end listing at roughly $5–6 billion — well below its 2021 peak. For NRIs who shifted money into India's startup story, the reset is the point.
articles.image_caption: The Bombay Stock Exchange in Mumbai; Razorpay has filed confidentially for an IPO (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: NRIs weighing India's fintech boom now have a marquee payments listing to price — but at a valuation a third below its peak, Razorpay is a test of whether the diaspora's India bets have to be repriced too.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Salesforce Just Paid $3.6 Billion for an AI Agent. It's Buying Insurance Against Its Own Obsolescence.
articles.excerpt: Marc Benioff's acquisition of Fin — the company formerly known as Intercom — is the 15th deal in a year-long spree. For the tens of thousands of Indians who build on Salesforce, the agentic shift is now the job.
articles.image_caption: andrewpeterfogg via flickr (BY-SA)
articles.nri_angle: Salesforce employs and certifies a vast Indian-origin engineering and admin workforce; its pivot from selling software seats to selling autonomous AI agents reshapes the careers of every NRI who built a living on the platform.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Gave Companies 12 Hours to Patch a Hacked System. AI Is the Reason the Clock Got So Short.
articles.excerpt: CERT-In's new blueprint says internet-facing 'crown jewel' systems with known exploited bugs should be fixed within half a day. The squeeze lands hardest on the Indian IT firms that run the diaspora's back office.
articles.image_caption: A data center server room; India's CERT-In has tightened breach-reporting to a 12-hour window (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The Indian IT majors and GCCs subject to CERT-In's faster patching rules also run payroll, banking and healthcare systems for clients across the US and UK — meaning the diaspora's data and the firms that employ NRIs both sit inside this tightening window.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Sundar Pichai Just Booked Google's First $100 Billion Quarter. The Real Test Ships Next.
articles.excerpt: Alphabet's CEO says AI is expanding Search, not eating it — and for the tens of thousands of Indian engineers inside Google, the milestone is a referendum on the bet that pays their salaries.
articles.image_caption: Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, who announced the company's first $100 billion quarter.
articles.nri_angle: Google's record quarter is a referendum on whether the company employing tens of thousands of Indian engineers has survived the AI transition — and on whether the next model, Gemini 3, keeps the machine that pays them running.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Canadian Pension Fund Just Bet $740 Million on Indian Server Farms. For NRI Investors, That's the Tell.
articles.excerpt: CPP Investments is buying into CtrlS Datacenters as India's data-center market races toward $13 billion — and the AI boom finally has an India-based infrastructure trade.
articles.image_caption: calix via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: When one of the world's most conservative pension funds pours $740 million into Indian data centers, it signals a credible, India-based AI-infrastructure trade for NRI investors — and a new wave of hyperscale engineering jobs that won't all sit in the United States.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: HCLTech Just Bought a Piece of the AI That Was Supposed to Kill It. The Target: India's Own Models.
articles.excerpt: A $1.5 billion bet on Sarvam AI turns India's sovereign-AI slogan into a balance-sheet commitment — and gives diaspora researchers a credible reason to look home.
articles.image_caption: TheStevieAwards via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: As Washington tightens who can touch frontier AI models, India's push for a sovereign-AI stack — now backed by HCLTech's stake in Sarvam — becomes both a source of new senior research jobs at home and a career hedge for Indian engineers inside US AI labs.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Adani Just Recruited an Apple Supplier to Build India's AI Hardware. The Bet Is That Compute Follows Cheap Power.
articles.excerpt: A new alliance between the Adani Group and Florida's Jabil aims to manufacture multi-gigawatt AI data-center racks inside India — the clearest sign yet that the country wants to build the machines the world's models run on, not just write the code.
articles.image_caption: Adani Group chairman Gautam Adani, whose conglomerate has partnered with U.S. manufacturer Jabil to build AI data-center hardware in India.
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs who have spent careers inside American data centers and chip supply chains, India's push to manufacture AI hardware at home opens a homecoming option that did not exist a year ago — and a fresh thesis for diaspora investors tracking Adani's stocks.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Wall Street Just Downgraded the Companies That Employ the Indian Diaspora. The Reason Should Worry Every IT Worker.
articles.excerpt: Morgan Stanley cut Accenture and turned cautious on the entire US IT-services industry, warning that AI spending is crowding out the consulting budgets that pay hundreds of thousands of Indian-origin professionals.
articles.image_caption: Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (CC)
articles.nri_angle: Accenture, Cognizant, Capgemini and the Indian IT majors employ vast numbers of Indian and Indian-American workers. A Wall Street downgrade of the whole industry is an early-warning signal about the career ground beneath the diaspora's feet.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Washington Told Anthropic to Cut Off Foreigners. Now India Is Asking Who Really Owns the AI It Runs On.
articles.excerpt: A U.S. government directive that locked non-citizens out of Anthropic's newest models has set off a sovereign-AI reckoning in Bengaluru — and a quiet warning for every Indian engineer building on a borrowed brain.
articles.image_caption: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, whose company suspended access to its newest models for foreign nationals after a U.S. government directive.
articles.nri_angle: For Indian engineers in the U.S. on visas and the Bengaluru teams that serve American startups, the episode is a blunt reminder that access to the AI models their jobs depend on can be revoked by a government directive overnight.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Tesla Just Handed Indian Families a Six-Seat EV. The Price Tag Tells You Who It's Really For.
articles.excerpt: Deliveries of the three-row Model Y L have begun in India at ₹62 lakh, with a cheaper rear-wheel-drive variant landing in July — Tesla's clearest signal yet that it is chasing the affluent urban family, not the mass market.
articles.image_caption: A 2025 Tesla Model Y; Tesla has begun delivering the six-seat Model Y L variant to customers in India.
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs weighing a return to India or buying a car for family back home, Tesla's pricing puts a familiar American badge within reach of the upper-middle class — but at a premium that reframes what 'affordable EV' means in India.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America Is About to Get Its First Real AI Law. It's Not Coming From Washington — and That's the Problem.
articles.excerpt: Colorado's AI Act takes effect June 30 and California's follows in August, even as Congress floats a bill to freeze state rules for three years. For the Indian engineers building the systems, the patchwork is now a compliance headache with their name on the commit.
articles.image_caption: kevin dooley via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: Indian-American engineers and founders building AI products now face a state-by-state thicket of discrimination and disclosure rules — turning algorithmic fairness from an abstract debate into code, audits, and legal exposure they personally have to ship.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: TCS Cut 12,000 Jobs From the Middle. The Layer That Built India's IT Industry Is the One AI Is Erasing.
articles.excerpt: Chandrasekaran says Tata Consultancy Services will soon run as many AI agents as people. For the diaspora, the pyramid that funded a generation of H-1B careers is being flattened from the inside.
articles.image_caption: Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran, who told shareholders AI will cut TCS hiring
articles.nri_angle: The Indian IT pyramid that has trained and exported tech talent to the US for three decades is being hollowed out at the middle, reshaping the career ladder for the next wave of would-be H-1B engineers and the families already here.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nikesh Arora Spent $30 Billion Rebuilding Palo Alto Networks for the Age of AI Agents
articles.excerpt: The CyberArk and Chronosphere deals bet that every AI agent now needs its own identity and its own guard. For Indian engineers, it is the clearest map yet of where security jobs are moving.
articles.image_caption: Palo Alto Networks chairman and CEO Nikesh Arora, who has led the company's $30 billion AI-security acquisition spree
articles.nri_angle: An Indian-origin CEO is reshaping the entire cybersecurity industry around agentic AI, and the skills shift he is betting on — identity and machine-to-machine security — is exactly where the next decade of Indian-American tech careers will be built.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Biggest EV Wave Yet Starts This Week. Ola's Collapse Shows Why Speed Was Never the Point.
articles.excerpt: Sixteen electric launches are lined up against seven new petrol models over nine months. The startup that once owned half the scooter market has lost more than half its volume — a cautionary tale for NRI investors chasing the India EV story.
articles.image_caption: Ola Electric scooters lined up at a showroom; the company's two-wheeler volumes fell more than 53% in FY26
articles.nri_angle: NRIs increasingly hold Indian EV stocks and watch the clean-mobility story as a proxy for India's growth — but the Ola Electric collapse is a hard lesson that disruption hype and durable execution are very different bets.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Took 120 of Its Hardest Science Startups to France. They Came Back With $100 Million in Deals.
articles.excerpt: At Bharat Innovates 2026 in Nice, IIT Madras spinouts including rocket-maker Agnikul and a hyperloop venture signed commercial MoUs — a bid to be seen as a builder of frontier tech, not the world's back office.
articles.image_caption: The main gate of the Indian Institute of Technology Madras in Chennai
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs weighing whether to move money — or themselves — back to India, deep-tech ventures finally signing real international contracts changes the calculus: the bet is no longer just on Indian IT services, but on Indian hard science with global customers.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Judge Killed Trump's $100,000 H-1B Fee. A Day Later, It Was Back. Tech's Indian Workforce Is on a Legal Seesaw.
articles.excerpt: A Boston judge ruled the six-figure visa fee an unlawful tax, then an appeals stay reinstated it — leaving the IT firms and Bay Area engineers who depend on H-1B caught between rulings.
articles.image_caption: A United States visa and entry stamps in a passport
articles.nri_angle: Indians receive more than 70% of H-1B visas, and the tech industry runs on them — so the whiplash of a $100,000 fee being struck down and then reinstated within a day directly governs whether thousands of engineers can keep, change, or take new jobs in the US.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nvidia Built a CPU 'for Agents, Not Humans.' Indian Engineers Are About to Build the Apps That Run on It.
articles.excerpt: Jensen Huang's new Vera processor is going into production just as India lines up $50 billion in AI data-center spending — putting the diaspora at both ends of the agentic-AI supply chain.
articles.image_caption: Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, pictured in 2025.
articles.nri_angle: Indian engineers write a huge share of the world's enterprise software and India is now building the data centers to run it — so Nvidia's agent-first chip lands squarely on the diaspora's turf.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: ISRO Hasn't Launched a Rocket Since January. A Return-to-Flight Is Now Weeks Away.
articles.excerpt: After two PSLV failures, India's space agency is targeting a late-June or early-July comeback — with the first uncrewed Gaganyaan test and a private Skyroot orbital launch waiting behind it.
articles.image_caption: An ISRO Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) on the pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota.
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs who treat ISRO milestones as a source of pride and increasingly as an investable space economy, the agency's return to flight is the credibility test that unlocks both.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Arvind Krishna Just Tied IBM to ServiceNow. The Bet: Companies Want Plumbing, Not Chatbots.
articles.excerpt: IBM's long-term alliance with ServiceNow targets the messy data and legacy code that stall enterprise AI — the exact work that keeps thousands of Indian engineers and IT-services firms employed.
articles.image_caption: IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna, pictured in 2025.
articles.nri_angle: The 'unglamorous' integration work IBM is betting on is precisely what employs tens of thousands of Indian engineers and props up the US revenue of TCS, Infosys and Wipro.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: SpaceX Just Paid $60 Billion for Cursor. The Coding Tool Half of Bengaluru Already Lives In.
articles.excerpt: Elon Musk's empire is buying the AI coding agent that automated the work of millions of engineers. For Indian developers who made Cursor a daily habit, the question is who owns their workflow now.
articles.image_caption: Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (CC)
articles.nri_angle: Cursor became the default coding tool inside Indian IT firms and Bay Area engineering teams stacked with Indian talent; an Elon Musk acquisition puts that daily workflow under new ownership just as AI is reshaping who gets hired.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Tata's Bigbasket Just Hired an Amazon Veteran to Win the 10-Minute Grocery War
articles.excerpt: Amit Nanda, who spent more than a decade building Amazon India, takes over a Tata-backed grocery giant fighting Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart for the right to deliver in minutes.
articles.image_caption: A worker packs groceries for delivery, the operational heart of India's fast-growing quick-commerce sector
articles.nri_angle: Quick commerce reshaped how families in India shop — including the parents NRIs order groceries for from abroad; a Tata-backed leadership change signals how seriously India's biggest conglomerate is fighting for the 10-minute delivery market the diaspora increasingly relies on.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Wipro Just Opened a Claude Lab in Bengaluru. The Company AI Was Supposed to Gut Is Now Its Best Customer.
articles.excerpt: India's third-largest IT firm will train 10,000 engineers on Anthropic's models — a tacit admission that the only way to survive AI deflation is to sell it.
articles.image_caption: Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (CC)
articles.nri_angle: Hundreds of thousands of Indian engineers — at Wipro's Bengaluru towers and on H-1B desks in New Jersey and the Bay Area — are watching their employers race to befriend the same AI that analysts say is eating their jobs.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Chip Startups Found Money This Year. Now They Want Something Harder: Customers and the Right to Stay Indian.
articles.excerpt: Funding quadrupled in five months, but founders heading to a Nice deep-tech stage warn that without domestic buyers and IP protection, the next round will be raised — and owned — abroad.
articles.image_caption: Nick Kenrick.. via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: NRI investors and returning chip engineers keep hearing that India's semiconductor story is finally real — but the founders living it say the ownership of that story is still up for grabs, and diaspora capital could decide whose flag flies over it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian Startup Says It Can Make AI Video in Four Steps Instead of Fifty. It's Giving the Model Away.
articles.excerpt: Avataar.ai's Varya, backed by the India AI Mission, claims a tenfold speed jump over global rivals — and will release as an open-weight model, betting that cheap and free beats Hollywood-grade and locked.
articles.image_caption: AI video generation, the field where Avataar.ai's open Varya model aims to compete on speed and cost (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: For NRI creators, founders, and small businesses, a free Indian video model that runs cheap could undercut the per-clip subscription costs of Western tools — and quietly tilt who gets to make slick content from a laptop in Edison or Wembley.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Qualcomm Wants to Buy Its Way Out of the Phone. The $10 Billion Target Is Jim Keller's Chip Startup.
articles.excerpt: Qualcomm is in talks to acquire Tenstorrent for as much as $10 billion — a bet on RISC-V silicon and one of the industry's most coveted engineers, days before its make-or-break AI investor day.
articles.image_caption: Tenstorrent CEO Jim Keller, the chip architect behind AMD's Zen and Apple's A-series, is the prize in Qualcomm's reported acquisition talks.
articles.nri_angle: Qualcomm employs thousands of Indian engineers across San Diego, Bengaluru and Hyderabad — a pivot from saturating smartphones to data-center AI silicon reshapes the career ladder and stock options for Indian chip professionals on both sides of the ocean.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Forbes Counted America's Most Successful Immigrants. 26 of the Top 250 Are Indian.
articles.excerpt: As the United States turns 250, Forbes' new ranking reads like a roll call of the diaspora — from four Big Tech CEOs to the venture capitalists quietly funding the next generation.
articles.image_caption: Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, one of 26 Indian-origin leaders named on Forbes' 2026 list of America's most successful immigrants.
articles.nri_angle: For every Indian American watching their kids choose between an engineering degree and a startup, the Forbes list is proof of a ceiling that no longer exists — and a map of who in the community now controls capital, code, and corporate boards.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Biggest Nvidia GPU Operator Is Going Public. For NRI Investors, It's the First Pure AI-Infrastructure Bet at Home.
articles.excerpt: Yotta Data Services is lining up a Mumbai IPO at a valuation of up to $6 billion, just as a $2.34 billion US partnership validates India's claim to be the next AI-compute hub.
articles.image_caption: Nvidia AI accelerators of the kind Yotta operates at scale across India (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: NRIs have long invested back home through Indian mutual funds and real estate; Yotta's listing offers the first liquid, public way to own a slice of India's AI-compute boom — the same buildout US hyperscalers are pouring $100 billion-plus into.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
